round: the tester's one failure: a wait answering about the previous run's terminating pod; fixed with a per-run name, which also closes the cross-role collision banked on dispatch://INFRA-215

proof.criterion: The tester's failure — following the section's own advice twice makes both waits answer about the previous run's dying pod, because a pod keeps its `job-name` label while it terminates. The role is told its workload is Ready when it is not, and the section then sends it to the one failure that announces nothing.
proof.surface: The live cluster from this role container: the defect reproduced with the published fixed name before changing anything.
proof.command: apply the section's Job under a fixed name ; wait create and Ready ; kubectl delete job ; apply the same manifest again at once ; kubectl get pod -l job-name=… ; both waits again
proof.observed: After the second apply the selector matched **two** pods, the new one `Pending` and the old one `Terminating`. `kubectl wait --for=create` returned **0 after 1 s naming the previous run's pod** (`…-qlhqg`, the one just deleted). The Ready wait ran 32 s and ended `pod/…-mmh4l condition met` *and* `Error from server (NotFound): pods "…-qlhqg" not found`, exit 1 — one answer about each pod. That is the tester's finding, measured independently before the fix rather than taken from the report.
proof.negativeControl: The reproduction is itself the control for the fix below: the same two commands, in the same shape, against a name that is fresh each run cannot match a terminating pod, because that pod never carried the label.

proof.criterion: The remedy: a name unique per run and per role, built once and substituted into both manifests, so every selector, the Service, its owner reference and the address carry it.
proof.surface: The live cluster, driving the published sequence in each shape the architect named, with the waits bounded at five seconds so a run that passes because the corpse had already gone is distinguishable from one that passes because the name is fresh.
proof.command: three re-run shapes back to back (apply, waits, delete, apply again at once); the shape where the delete is issued while the pod is still Running and the next run starts at once; and the paused shape, a ten-second gap where the Service steps would sit
proof.observed: Every shape: exactly **one** pod matched the selector, `--for=create` exited 0 within its five seconds naming that pod, and the Ready wait exited 0 naming the **same** pod — never a second one, never a `NotFound`. Re-runs 1 to 3: pods `pq8qj`, `xjqcj`, `r9cb8`, each its own run's. Delete-while-Running: the next run answered on `nk8hf`, its own, one second after its apply. Paused shape: create and Ready both 0, one pod, and the workload's own log line read (`database system is ready to accept connections`). Two names generated from the published line in the same second differ (`a7f4c5` / `f7aec2`).
proof.negativeControl: The five-second bound is the control the architect asked for: with the old fixed name the create wait also returned inside one second, but on the corpse — so speed alone proves nothing and the check is *which pod was named*, which is why every run above records the pod's own suffix on both waits. Housekeeping: every Job carried a fifteen-minute deadline and a five-minute cleanup window, was named for this issue, and was deleted by hand; the final listing shows nothing of mine.

proof.criterion: The rename must reach every place the name appears, since a Service whose selector does not follow it points at nothing — and that failure reads exactly like the missing reachability label, the one cause this section says announces nothing.
proof.surface: The published text itself, read as the sequence substitutes it.
proof.command: the section's two manifests and its sh block extracted and expanded as the sequence expands them (`sed "s|<workload>|$workload|g"`), then the Job applied from that expansion in every run above
proof.observed: Every `<workload>` occurrence is inside the two manifests — the Job's `metadata.name`, the Service's `metadata.name`, its `ownerReferences` entry and its `selector: {job-name: …}` — so one substitution with `g` carries them all, and the sequence's own lines use `"$workload"` for both waits, the logs, the delete and the address the reachability check builds. The runs above were applied from exactly that expansion, so the Job half is proven under the new naming rather than under a hand-written name. The label bullet's diagnostic command uses `"$workload"` too.
proof.negativeControl: The dangerous half-rename is the one the architect named: a Service selector left behind would produce a Service with no endpoints, whose symptom is the reachability check timing out — identical to the missing label. It cannot occur here because the Service carries no literal name at all: every occurrence is the same placeholder the one substitution fills.

filesChanged: docs/kubernetes.md: the naming paragraph (now a name per run, with the re-run measurement in it), the sequence's name line and every step that uses it, the Job manifest's comment, and the label bullet's diagnostic command.
trickyParts: The name must be unique per run *and* per role of one issue, and two role containers can generate one in the same second, so the suffix is six random characters from `python3 -c 'import secrets; print(secrets.token_hex(3))'` rather than a timestamp. The section already uses `python3` for the reachability check, so nothing new is required of the image.
deviations: The naming clause changed, which is the thing the architect asked to be told about: a per-run name closes the cross-role collision he holds on dispatch://INFRA-215 as well as this defect, so that item is paid for here and he can retire it. He is told by Envoy.

Neither of the other two remedies was taken: `--for=delete` before the apply fixes the re-run case while making the collision case worse (a role would wait on another role's live workload), and selecting by the uid the sequence already reads is precise but adds a step to a sequence a reader follows by hand.
openQuestions: Specification acceptance 1 to 4 remain the live proof after a person applies dispatch://INFRA-206: the Service steps are refused here on the read, so no workload of this namespace has a name on the network yet.
discoveredComplexity: The old race was lost two times in four at a five-second bound, by the tester's count — which is how a line gets written, run once, seen to work, and shipped. Every wait in this section is now judged by which pod it named rather than by its exit status.
